name: Ahoah
title: Son of Bela, Benjamin's firstborn
summary: Ahoah belonged to the earliest generation of the tribe of Benjamin as a son of Bela, Benjamin's firstborn. His name is preserved in the genealogy in 1 Chronicles, where the descendants of Benjamin are documented with regard to tribal affiliation and inheritance lines. Although there are no individual stories about Ahoah in the biblical text, most evidence points to him being the origin of the patronymic term 'Ahohite' – a surname later associated with prominent warriors among King David's men. Through his lineage, Ahoah represents an important link between Benjamin's earliest tribal history and the military tradition that characterized this tribe throughout Israel's history.
roles: Ancestor in the tribe of Benjamin
Possible origin of the Ahohite clan

keyEvents.title: Listed in Benjamin's genealogy
keyEvents.description: Ahoah is mentioned among the sons of Bela, Benjamin's firstborn, in the genealogy that documents the main family lines within the tribe of Benjamin. This list includes both Bela's sons and further descendants, serving to preserve the tribe's identity and inheritance rights.

versions.summary: Ahoah was a son of Bela, who was the firstborn son of Benjamin. He is mentioned in the genealogies in 1 Chronicles as part of the tribe of Benjamin. Ahoah is a relatively little-known biblical figure, but his place in the genealogies shows his significance in Israel's tribal history.
versions.title: Son of Bela from the tribe of Benjamin
versions.reason: [major] Ahoah is himself included in his own genealogy, which is incorrect. A person cannot be their own sibling.; [minor] 'gera' appears twice in the genealogy. It could refer to two different people with the same name, but more likely it is a duplication error.; [major] The genealogies based on 1 Chron 8:3-5 mention Addar, Gera, Abihud, Abishua, Naaman, Shephuphan and Huram. The names vary between different sources, but the list should reflect what actually appears in the text. 'Ahoah' should be removed from his own genealogy.; [minor] Calling Ahoah a 'patriarch' may be misleading. He was not a patriarch in the traditional biblical sense (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob). A more appropriate role would be 'ancestor' or 'clan head' within the tribe of Benjamin.; [minor] The four keyEvents are somewhat overlapping and repetitive. They all refer to the same passage in 1 Chron 8. It would be more informative to reduce them to fewer, more distinct events.; [major] The reference to 1 Chron 7:6-11 primarily concerns Benjamin's sons in a different context and does not mention Ahoah directly. This event is misleading as a key event specifically for Ahoah.; [minor] 'patriarchs' is technically acceptable since Ahoah belongs to the generation after Benjamin (Jacob's son), but it is borderline. The patriarchal period usually refers to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Nevertheless, since Ahoah is in the generation immediately following Jacob, it can be defended.; [minor] The summary is fine, but could mention that the name Ahoah may possibly be connected to the patronymic designation 'Ahohite' which appears elsewhere in the OT (e.g., 2 Sam 23:9, 28).

versions.summary: Ahoah was a son of Bela, the firstborn son of Benjamin. He is mentioned in the genealogies in 1 Chronicles as part of the tribe of Benjamin. Although Ahoah is a relatively little-known biblical figure, his name is likely connected to the patronymic designation 'Ahohite,' which appears in connection with several of David's prominent warriors. His place in the genealogies testifies to his significance as a patriarch within Israel's tribal history.
versions.title: Son of Bela from the tribe of Benjamin
versions.reason: [major] Ahoah is mentioned in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 8 as part of the tribe of Benjamin. Chronologically, he is most likely placed in the period associated with the settlement in Canaan or the time of the judges, not the patriarchal era. The patriarchal era primarily covers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Benjamin himself was a patriarch, but Ahoah belongs several generations later and should be situated in a later epoch.; [major] In 1 Chron 8:3-4, the sons of Bela are mentioned, but Ahoah is specifically named in verse 4, not verse 1. Verse 1 concerns Benjamin and his firstborn Bela. The references should be adjusted so that verse 4 is included (which it already is), but verse 1 deals with Benjamin, not directly with Ahoah. Verse 3 mentions Addar, Gera, and Abihud – Ahoah is mentioned in verse 4.; [minor] The list of siblings varies somewhat between different translations and textual traditions. 'Shefufan' and 'Huram' may have variants (e.g., Shefufam/Shuppim and Huram/Hiram). It is worth verifying that these names correspond with the Hebrew base text in 1 Chron 8:3-5.; [minor] The summary is good but could be strengthened with a bit more contextual information about Ahoah's place within the tribal system and the possible connection to the Ahohites, without repeating formulations from earlier versions.; [minor] The source type of this footnote is marked as 'theological', but the content deals primarily with textual variations and tradition history, which is more linguistic or text-critical than theological.

versions.summary: Ahoah was one of the sons of Bela, Benjamin's firstborn, and thus belonged to one of the prominent family lines within the tribe of Benjamin. He is listed in the genealogy in 1 Chronicles, where Bela's descendants are recorded as part of the tribal history of Benjamin. Although little is known about Ahoah as an individual, his name likely gave rise to the term 'Ahitite', which is associated with several of King David's notable warriors. As a forefather of such a warrior lineage, his place in the genealogy testifies to lasting influence within Israel's tribal structure and military tradition.
versions.title: Son of Bela from the tribe of Benjamin
versions.reason: [major] Ahoah is mentioned in genealogies that trace back to the sons and grandsons of Benjamin, placing him in the patriarchal period rather than the time of the judges. Benjamin was one of Jacob's sons, and Bela was Benjamin's firstborn. As a son of Bela, Ahoah therefore belongs to the patriarchal era.; [minor] The two key events overlap significantly – both concern the same genealogy in 1 Chr 8. It would have been better to combine them into a single event or give them clearly distinct angles to avoid repetition.; [minor] The names of the siblings should be carefully verified against 1 Chr 8:3-5. Some translations render 'Shefufan' as 'Shefufam' or 'Shuppim', and 'Huram' as 'Hiram'. It may also be discussed whether 'Gera' here is the same as in other lists. The name forms should be consistent with the rest of the database.; [minor] The summary is good, but the third version should be phrased differently from the two preceding ones to ensure variety and freshness in the text. The current text has certain similarities with earlier versions in its opening formulation.

footnotes.text: The name Ahoah (אֲחוֹחַ) is likely connected to the patronymic designation 'Ahohite' (אֲחֹחִי), which appears in connection with several of King David's prominent warriors, including Dodo son-of-Ahohi (2 Sam 23:9; 1 Chr 11:12) and Salma the Ahohite (2 Sam 23:28; 1 Chr 11:29). This suggests that Ahoah was the ancestor of a warrior clan that gained significant influence several generations later.

The genealogies in 1 Chronicles 8 were likely compiled after the Babylonian exile, with the purpose of restoring and documenting tribal affiliation and inheritance rights among those who returned. The tribe of Benjamin held a special position since, together with Judah, it formed the core of the restored community in Judah.

There are noticeable variations in the lists of Bela's sons between 1 Chr 8:3-5, 1 Chr 7:6-12, and Gen 46:21. These differences may be due to different tradition layers, scribal variants over time, or that the lists refer to different generational levels within the same family line.

Within rabbinic tradition, the tribe of Benjamin was considered especially brave and warlike, as reflected in Jacob's blessing (Gen 49:27), where Benjamin is compared to a ravenous wolf. That Ahoah's descendants possibly became known as skilled warriors in David's time fits into this broader picture of the tribe of Benjamin as a warrior tribe in Israel.

The tribe of Benjamin held a unique position in Israel's history, notably as the tribe to which Israel's first king Saul belonged (1 Sam 9:1-2). The genealogies that include Ahoah helped preserve and legitimize these tribal lines, which became especially important for identity building after the Babylonian exile.
